title: Ghana Sugar Bread
localName: Sugar bread — butter bread, sweet bread
author: Yummy Medley
desc: Soft, sweet and pillowy — proofed yeast must be foamy and bubbled up, and the dough rises till it doubles in size.
longDesc: The sweetened loaf Ghanaians eat for breakfast, distinguished in the literature from unsweetened tea bread. Three hundred and ninety grams of bread flour with half a cup of sugar, three quarters of a cup of scalded flour, a sachet of active dry yeast, a teaspoon of salt and an eighth of a teaspoon of ascorbic acid. The yeast is proofed in a cup of water at 105 to 115 degrees with a teaspoon of sugar for ten minutes, and it should be foamy and should have bubbled up. Kneading takes fifteen minutes, until it is smooth to touch and not sticky, then it rises until doubled, about an hour. Six balls, a second rise, and thirty to thirty-five minutes at 350.
ingredients: 1/2 cup sugar, plus 1 tsp for proofing the yeast
3/4 cup scalded flour — see the note, the source does not define this
steps: Proof the yeast: combine 1 cup of water at 105 to 115 degrees Fahrenheit with 1 teaspoon of sugar and the yeast, and leave 10 minutes.
It should be foamy and should have bubbled up. If it is not, the yeast is dead — start again.
Combine the bread flour, the 1/2 cup of sugar, the scalded flour, the salt and the ascorbic acid.
Add the proofed yeast mixture and bring together into a dough. Keep the yeast and the salt apart in the bowl until mixing, because the salt will weaken the yeast.
Knead 15 minutes. It should be smooth to touch after kneading and not sticky.
Leave to rise till it doubles in size — usually about 1 hour.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit.
Divide into 6 balls and arrange them in the pan.
Leave for the second rise, until doubled.
chefTips: Foamy and bubbled up is the proof cue, and it is the ten minutes that saves you three hours. Flat water after ten minutes means dead yeast.
Smooth to touch and not sticky is the kneading endpoint, after fifteen minutes. Another printing gives the same cue as the dough no longer sticking to the sides of the bowl.
Doubled in size, about an hour. Every documented printing of this bread gives doubling as the cue rather than relying on the clock, which is why it publishes.
Keep the yeast and salt apart in the bowl until you mix, because salt weakens yeast. That instruction comes from a second printing and is worth importing.
Water at 105 to 115 degrees. Hotter kills the yeast; colder will not wake it. Use a thermometer the first time.

Be aware that 'scalded flour' is never defined in the source and nothing on the page explains how to make it. It is a yudane- or tangzhong-style hot-water flour paste, but that reading is not the source's.
Ascorbic acid is a dough conditioner at an eighth of a teaspoon. Vitamin C powder works; leaving it out gives a slightly less springy crumb.
commonMistakes: Skipping the ten-minute proof and discovering dead yeast later.
Mixing the salt straight into the yeast.
Under-kneading, so the dough stays sticky.
sources: THREE PRINTINGS EXIST AND THEY DISAGREE SUBSTANTIALLY. The version published above is printing (a), which is the only one of the three with a complete, internally consistent set of quantities and times.

(a) 'Ghana Sugar Bread Rolls', yummowmedley print page at yummymedley.com/wprm_print/ghana-sugar-bread-rolls. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Yummy Medley' — THE SITE'S OWN NAME, not a person. No date. Yield as printed: 6 rolls. Ingredients TWO-PASS: '390 g 2 2/3 cups bread flour'; '1/2 cup of sugar'; '3/4 cup scalded flour'; '2 1/4 tsp 1 sachet active dry yeast'; '1 tsp salt'; '1/8 tsp ascorbic acid'. Method: yeast in 1 cup water at 105-115°F plus 1 tsp sugar for 10 minutes; knead '15 minutes'; rise 'till it doubles in size (usually about 1 hour)'; knead 5 minutes more; preheat to 350°F; 6 balls; second rise until doubled; bake '30-35 minutes'.

A GAP IN PRINTING (a), flagged and not filled: 'SCALDED FLOUR' IS NEVER DEFINED ON THE PAGE and nothing explains how to make it. Three quarters of a cup of it is a substantial share of the recipe. No definition is asserted; the tips name the likely technique and label it as a reading rather than as the source's words.

(b) 'Agege Bread (Ghana Sugar Bread) Recipe', coquitlamheritage.ca. CREDIT LINE AS PRINTED: 'This recipe was provided by our Artist in Residence, Delali Adiamah.' No date, no yield beyond '4 equal parts'; the site operator is not identified on the page. Opening, TWO-PASS: 'Agege Bread, also known as Sweet Bread, Ghana Sugar Bread- Butter Bread, has a soft, sweet, buttery and pillowy taste and texture.' A NAMING FLAG: 'AGEGE' IS THE NIGERIAN NAME, after the Lagos suburb, and this page conflates it with Ghana sugar bread. Ingredients TWO-PASS, as printed: '3cups (384g) of all-purpose flour'; '1/4cup (50g) of sugar'; '1/4cup (57g) of melted butter'; '1tsp (5g) of salt'; '1/2tsp (2.5g) of nutmeg'; '1/2tsp = 2.5g of butter flavour'; '3/4 - 1 cup (6-8fl oz or 177-236ml) of warm water'; '2tsp (10g) of active dry yeast'. Its cues, verbatim: 'Keep yeast and salt apart in the bowl because the salt will weaken the yeast'; 'Knead for 15-20 minutes...It is ready when the dough is no longer sticking to the sides of the bowl'; 'proof for an hour or doubled in size'; 'After 45 mins the dough should double in size, remove the film'. ITS BAKE INSTRUCTION IS INCOMPLETE AS PRINTED: 'Reduce heat and bake at 325 degrees for 15-20 mins depending on how brown you want it' — THE TEMPERATURE IT IS REDUCED FROM IS NEVER GIVEN. Flagged, not reconstructed.

(c) 'Vegan Ghanaian Butter Bread', thecanadianafrican.com. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'By Afia' — see the attribution note at GHA109 regarding Afia Amoako. No date. Yield: the page says 'Serves: 10-12 slices'; one pass of a variant URL said 'One loaf'. Ingredients TWO-PASS: '1/2 tbsp dry instant yeast'; '2 tbsp sugar'; '1 1/4 cup soy milk'; '2.5 cup all-purpose flour (360g)'; '1 cup bread flour (140g)'; '2/3 cup vegan butter'; '1 tsp of salt'; '1/2 tsp nutmeg'; '1 tsp of vanilla essence'. Cues: bloom the yeast 10 minutes 'till it blooms', cue 'frothy'; knead 10 minutes; 'Let it rise in an oiled bowl for about 45 minutes', one pass adding 'until doubled'; second rise 30 minutes; 'Bake at 325°F for 25 minutes, then 300°F for another 10 minutes'. THREE MISPRINTS IN (c), flagged and not corrected: the ingredient list says 1/2 tbsp yeast but the method says '1 tbsp of dry yeast'; the method says 'almond milk' where NO almond milk is listed; and the method blooms the yeast with '1 tbsp' of sugar while the list totals 2 tbsp. A fourth reading of the same recipe elsewhere gives a 40-minute bake at 325°F with a steam pan, against this page's 25-plus-10. Cultural note, one pass only: 'Traditionally bread in Ghana is made with margarine.'

THE DISAGREEMENT, unreconciled: (a) kneads 15 then 5 minutes and bakes 30-35 minutes at 350°F with bread flour, scalded flour and ascorbic acid and no fat at all; (b) kneads 15-20 minutes and bakes 15-20 minutes at 325°F with all-purpose flour, melted butter, nutmeg and butter flavour; (c) kneads 10 minutes and bakes 25 minutes at 325°F plus 10 at 300°F with a blend of flours, vegan butter, nutmeg and vanilla. These are three materially different breads and none is corrected toward another.

THE FERMENTATION RULE IS SATISFIED by all three printings, which is why this publishes: every one of them gives DOUBLING as the rise endpoint rather than a bare elapsed time, and (a) and (c) both give an observable yeast-proof cue as well — 'foamy and should have bubbled up' and 'frothy'.

A SOURCE REFUSED under that same rule, and recorded: a Betumi 'Sugar Bread Recipe (Working Draft)' dated 18 March 2007 is self-described as untested, and its final proof is '4-8 hours (Ghana standard is 8 hours)' with NO observable cue. A second Betumi post of 5 March 2007 concerns Ghanaian TEA bread, not sugar bread. Neither is used.

THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN THE TWO BREADS, from Whitby's 1968 CSIR-FRI survey and TWO-PASS: 'There are two main varieties of bread, Tea Bread, which is not sweetened, and Sugar Bread.' Also from Whitby, on how it was baked: 'Beehive-shaped ovens are used in many areas for baking it. Firewood is burned inside the oven then raked out and the bread cooked by residual heat. There are also modern bakeries in most large towns which make bread for sale.' Whitby gives NO RECIPE.

NO GHANAIAN-AUTHORED SUGAR BREAD RECIPE with full quantities was found under a personal byline: (a) is bylined by a site, (b) by a credit line on a Canadian heritage-society blog, and (c) by a first name only. That is disclosed rather than smoothed over.
storage: 3 days at room temperature in a bag, or 3 months frozen.
reheating: A warm oven, or toast it. It is excellent toasted with butter.
healthBenefits: Bread flour's higher gluten content gives more protein than all-purpose.
No dairy in this printing, so it suits the lactose-intolerant.
Yeast fermentation improves the mineral availability of the flour.
Lower in fat than the butter-bread printings, which carry up to two thirds of a cup.
culturalNote: Sugar bread with a Milo or a bowl of hausa koko is the Ghanaian breakfast, bought warm from a woman with a basin on her head, and the beehive wood-fired ovens Whitby described in 1968 are still going in parts of the country. That the Nigerian name Agege gets attached to it in print is a small example of how West African food gets flattened once it crosses the Atlantic.
